course.title: Innovation, Entrepreneurship and Career Development
course.description: Develops opportunity recognition, value creation, experimentation, business-model reasoning, financial literacy, execution and career self-management.

outcomes.text: Identify meaningful problems and evaluate opportunities using evidence rather than assumption.
Develop value propositions and business-model hypotheses for defined users or stakeholders.
Design low-cost experiments to test demand, feasibility and key assumptions.
Interpret basic unit economics, cash needs, risk and ethical implications of a venture or project.
Build an execution and career-development plan grounded in evidence, reflection and measurable next actions.

lessons.title: Problem discovery and opportunity recognition
objectives: Gather evidence of a problem's frequency and importance
lessons.teaching_material: Entrepreneurial work begins with understanding a problem before committing to a solution. A useful problem statement identifies who experiences the problem, in what context, how often, what consequence follows and what people do today. Opportunity quality depends on more than novelty: the problem should matter enough that a stakeholder is willing to change behavior, allocate time, spend money or support a better alternative. Interviews and observation are evidence-gathering tools, not opportunities to persuade people to like an idea.
lessons.activity: Conduct three problem interviews without pitching a solution. Record concrete examples, current workarounds, frequency, consequence and evidence that the problem is important.

self_check.q: Why avoid pitching during problem interviews?
self_check.a: Pitching encourages politeness and hypothetical approval instead of revealing how people actually behave and what they currently struggle with.

self_check.q: What is stronger evidence than someone saying an idea sounds good?
self_check.a: Observed behavior, current spending, repeated workarounds, time loss or a concrete commitment to try or pay for a solution.

lessons.title: Value propositions and stakeholder outcomes
lessons.teaching_material: A value proposition explains why a defined stakeholder would choose a new option over the status quo. Features describe what a product or service contains; outcomes describe the improvement the user expects, such as saved time, reduced risk, higher revenue or better learning. Strong propositions identify the target user, important job or problem, promised outcome and relevant evidence. Different stakeholders may value different outcomes even when they interact with the same product.
lessons.activity: Write three value propositions for one idea aimed at three distinct stakeholders, then list the evidence required to validate each proposition.

self_check.q: What is the difference between a feature and an outcome?
self_check.a: A feature is a characteristic of the offering; an outcome is the change or benefit the stakeholder actually values.

self_check.q: Why might one product need multiple value propositions?
self_check.a: Different stakeholders can have different problems, incentives and definitions of value.

lessons.title: Business-model components and assumptions
objectives: Map how value is created and sustained
lessons.teaching_material: A business model links customers or beneficiaries, value proposition, channels, activities, resources, partners, costs and revenue or funding. Early models are hypotheses rather than facts. The most dangerous assumptions are those that must be true for the model to work but are not yet supported by evidence. Teams should identify these assumptions explicitly and test the highest-risk ones before investing heavily in product features, branding or infrastructure.
lessons.activity: Build a one-page business-model map and mark each assumption by importance and evidence strength; choose the top three assumptions for testing.

self_check.q: Why call an early business model a hypothesis?
self_check.a: Its customer behavior, economics and delivery assumptions have not yet been validated by sufficient real-world evidence.

self_check.q: Which assumptions should be tested first?
self_check.a: Those that are essential to success and currently supported by the least reliable evidence.

lessons.title: Market structure, competition and alternatives
objectives: Define a market from customer choice
lessons.teaching_material: Competition includes any alternative a customer can choose to solve the same problem, including doing nothing or using a manual workaround. Market analysis should therefore begin with customer behavior rather than a list of companies that look similar. Segment size matters, but so do willingness to switch, buying process, regulation, distribution and switching costs. A credible market argument states assumptions and sources instead of presenting a large headline market number as guaranteed demand.
lessons.activity: Create an alternatives map covering direct competitors, substitutes, internal/manual solutions and the status quo; explain why a user would switch or refuse to switch.

self_check.q: Is 'do nothing' a competitor?
self_check.a: Yes, when the user can tolerate the problem rather than adopt a new solution.

self_check.q: Why can a huge total market be misleading?
self_check.a: The relevant reachable segment may be much smaller because of behavior, geography, regulation, distribution or willingness to pay.

lessons.title: Testing assumptions with evidence
lessons.teaching_material: A good validation experiment is designed to change a decision. It states the assumption, expected behavior, method, success threshold and what will happen if the result fails. Behavioral evidence such as sign-ups, completed trials, deposits, repeat use or signed letters of intent is generally stronger than compliments or hypothetical survey answers. Experiments should be as small and inexpensive as possible while still producing evidence relevant to the risky assumption.
lessons.activity: Design a seven-day experiment for one risky assumption, including metric, success threshold, sample source, ethical constraints and decision rule.

self_check.q: What makes an experiment falsifiable?
self_check.a: It has a result that could clearly show the assumption is not sufficiently supported.

self_check.q: Why prefer behavioral evidence?
self_check.a: Actual actions usually reveal commitment more reliably than hypothetical statements about future behavior.

lessons.title: Minimum viable experiments and learning loops
objectives: Separate MVP learning from feature quantity
Use evidence to iterate or stop
lessons.teaching_material: A minimum viable experiment is the smallest credible way to learn whether a key assumption holds. It may be a landing page, concierge service, prototype, mock workflow or manual process rather than a full product. The objective is validated learning, not appearing finished. After each experiment, teams compare results with the predefined threshold, explain anomalies and decide to continue, change the assumption, redesign the test or stop pursuing that path.
lessons.activity: Turn a proposed six-month build into a two-week learning sequence containing three progressively stronger experiments.

self_check.q: Does an MVP always mean a small software product?
self_check.a: No. It can be any minimal artifact or service capable of testing a key assumption with real users.

self_check.q: Why define thresholds before seeing results?
self_check.a: Predefined thresholds reduce the temptation to reinterpret weak results as success after the fact.

lessons.title: Revenue, costs, contribution and cash
lessons.teaching_material: Revenue is not profit and accounting profit is not the same as available cash. Unit economics examine what is earned and what variable cost is incurred per unit, transaction or customer. Contribution margin helps determine whether growth improves or worsens economics before fixed costs. Cash planning asks when money enters and leaves, because a venture can appear profitable on paper while running out of cash before customers pay. Assumptions should be tested with ranges rather than one optimistic forecast.
lessons.activity: Build a simple twelve-month model with price, customers, variable cost, fixed cost, contribution margin and monthly cash balance; run optimistic, base and downside cases.

self_check.q: What is contribution margin in simple terms?
self_check.a: Revenue remaining after variable costs, available to cover fixed costs and eventually profit.

self_check.q: How can a profitable business run out of cash?
self_check.a: Cash payments can occur before cash receipts, or growth can consume working capital faster than it is replenished.

lessons.title: Risk, ethics and sustainable value creation
objectives: Evaluate whether value creation imposes unacceptable harm
lessons.teaching_material: Entrepreneurship creates value only when benefits are not achieved by shifting hidden costs or unacceptable harm onto others. Risk analysis should consider customers, workers, suppliers, investors, communities and the environment. Ethical questions include data use, misleading claims, discrimination, safety, labor conditions and environmental externalities. A responsible venture defines limits and controls early because incentives become harder to change after revenue, growth targets and organizational routines are established.
lessons.activity: Create a stakeholder-risk register for a venture idea with harm scenario, affected group, likelihood, impact, mitigation and a red-line condition that would stop deployment.

self_check.q: What is an externality?
self_check.a: A cost or benefit created by an activity that falls on people who are not fully represented in the transaction.

self_check.q: Why define red lines early?
self_check.a: Precommitment reduces the chance that growth pressure later normalizes unacceptable harm.

lessons.title: Execution systems, teams and communication
lessons.teaching_material: Execution improves when broad goals become measurable outcomes, owners, deadlines and review rhythms. Teams need clarity about who decides, who contributes and how disagreements are resolved. Meetings should create decisions, coordination or learning rather than simply consume time. Early-stage leadership also requires communicating uncertainty honestly: a team can act decisively while still distinguishing validated facts from assumptions and updating plans when new evidence appears.
lessons.activity: Create a six-week execution board for the course project with outcomes, owners, weekly evidence targets, decision points and retrospective questions.

self_check.q: What is a useful owner for a task?
self_check.a: One person who is clearly accountable for ensuring the task reaches its defined outcome, even when others contribute.

self_check.q: Why separate facts from assumptions in execution reviews?
self_check.a: It prevents teams from treating untested beliefs as settled reality and helps prioritize learning.

lessons.title: Career capital, portfolio and next-step planning
objectives: Identify evidence of skills and capability
lessons.teaching_material: Career development is stronger when students build evidence of capability rather than relying only on self-description. Career capital can include technical skill, domain knowledge, communication, trusted relationships, projects and a record of reliable execution. A portfolio should show the problem, the student's role, process, evidence and result without revealing confidential material. A practical development plan defines a target direction, current gaps, experiments, networking actions and review dates rather than assuming one irreversible career path.
lessons.activity: Create a one-page career thesis plus a ninety-day plan containing one portfolio artifact, one skills target, five relevant conversations and measurable application or project milestones.

self_check.q: What makes a portfolio artifact credible?
self_check.a: It shows observable work, the problem addressed, the student's contribution, process and evidence of result or learning.

self_check.q: Why treat a career plan as experiments?
self_check.a: Students learn about fit, demand and strengths through action and can update direction as evidence accumulates.

assessments.title: Problem and Opportunity Evidence Portfolio
assessments.instructions: Document a real problem using interviews or observation, current alternatives, stakeholder evidence and a testable value proposition.

assessments.title: Validation and Economics Experiment
assessments.instructions: Run one ethical low-cost validation experiment and submit results plus a simple unit-economics and cash scenario model.

assessments.title: Venture and Career Execution Capstone
assessments.instructions: Present an evidence-based opportunity or innovation proposal and a ninety-day execution/career plan, including risks, assumptions and next experiments.
